[MUQATIL:11:53-55/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | The people of Hud say he brought no clear proof that God had sent him to them.
[MUQATIL:11:53-55/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | They mean they will not stop worshipping idols merely because Hud says so, and they will not believe that he is a messenger.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Bare رويد occupies the position of a verb and means أرود in commands such as رويد زيدا.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | رويد can modify an explicit verbal noun as an adverb, or stand alone with the verbal noun omitted; with an expressed noun it can function in more than one way.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The attached kaf in رويدك specifies or emphasizes the addressee, distinguishing a particular listener when the form itself does not mark person or number.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | rejects | The kaf is neither a subject marker nor a noun: the implicit command subject is a doer, and treating kaf as a noun creates impossible constructions.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | In هلم لك, unlike رويدك, kaf is a genitive noun after لام; its meaning still adds specification or emphasis.
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | With a hidden nominative addressee, coordination and emphasis are smoother when that pronoun is made explicit, as in رويدكم أنتم وعبد الله. | mentions 5:24, 2:35
[SIBAWAYH:تقولرويدزيداوإنماتريدأرودزيدا|قالالهذلى#95/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A visible noun cannot coordinate directly with the genitive kaf in هلم لك; it can instead coordinate with the understood nominative addressee, made explicit by أنت.
[TAB-FULL:v12p446/r1] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Hud's people say he brought them no clear explanation or proof for his claims, so they will not concede that he truthfully calls them to worship God alone or that he is a prophet.
[TAB-FULL:v12p446/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | They will not abandon their deities because of what Hud says or on account of his words.
[TAB-FULL:v12p446/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | They say they do not believe or affirm Hud's claim to prophethood and a message from God to them.
[IBNABIHATIM:v6p2046/r1] IBNABIHATIM, d. 327 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Said ibn Jubayr glosses believers here as those who accept the truth.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p445#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | They deny that Hud brought a clear proof distinguishing truth from falsehood; this is slander, transgression, and refusal to accept evidence.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v11p445#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Here عن means by, as the prepositions عن and باء can alternate; the same usage occurs in 7:187 and 25:59. | mentions 7:187, 25:59
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:11:52-55/r4] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | They denied Hud's prophethood and claimed he had brought no clear proof.
[JISHUMI:v5p3513/r12] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The people of Ad claim that Hud brought no proof or miracle they could acknowledge; the claim is false because reflection reveals the proof, while doubts, imitation of leaders, and false premises divert them from considering it.
[JISHUMI:v5p3513/r13] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | They say they will not stop worshipping idols simply because Hud says their worship is false and commands them to leave it.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p183/r1] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | They tell Hūd that he has brought no clear proof or argument for his claim.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p183/r2] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | They will not abandon their gods merely because Hūd says so.
[BAGHAWI-FULL:v4p183/r3] BAGHAWI-FULL, d. 516 · author | holds | They say they will not believe Hūd.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p381#2/r1] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Their claim that Hūd brought no clear proof is a lie and denial, like Quraysh demanding a sign despite the Prophet’s many signs.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p381#2/r2] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | عن قولك is circumstantial: they will not abandon their gods in response to Hūd’s words, and they do not consider people like themselves fit to believe him.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v2p381#2/r3] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Their words aim to extinguish Hūd’s hope that they will accept his call.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p180#3/r1] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The people of Hūd mean that he brought no sign compelling them to believe; in their blindness they deny that his miracles qualify as signs.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p180#3/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | Their denial resembles Quraysh calling the Quran magic or poetry.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p180#3/r3] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | A Prophetic hadith says each prophet received signs like those by which people believed; this entails that Hūd and the other messengers had miracles, even if none are specified here.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v3p180#3/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | They will not abandon their idols because of Hūd’s statement, which they regard as unsupported by a sign.
[TABRISI:11:50-60#2/r10] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They worship idols because they think these bring them near God, Satan promises worldly favor through them, or anthropomorphist ideas lead them to make idols in the imagined divine form.
[TABRISI:11:50-60#2/r11] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | Their declaration means that they do not believe or affirm Hud's message.
[TABRISI:11:50-60#2/r7] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The people say Hud brought no clear proof or miracle that would establish his truthfulness.
[TABRISI:11:50-60#2/r8] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | One grammatical explanation makes “ʿan” stand in place of “bāʾ,” so the meaning is “because of your statement.”
[TABRISI:11:50-60#2/r9] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | They reject the proof because they imitate ancestors and leaders, dismiss its bearer without examining the evidence, doubt its validity, and hold false premises leading them to deny it.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p438/r1] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أبو زكريا | reports | Abū Zakariyyā says ʿan fundamentally indicates passing beyond: speech reaches a listener from someone, and turning from Zayd means passing him.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p438/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · أبو زكريا | reports | Abū Zakariyyā says ʿan is a preposition unless preceded by min; after min it is a noun because one preposition does not govern another.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p438/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | reports | ʿAn can carry the sense of bi, 'because of' or 'by'. | mentions 53:3
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p117#3/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Hūd's people say he brought no clear proof or argument.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p117#3/r2] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | Their gods are the idols they worship.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v4p117#3/r3] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | The phrase means they will not leave their idols because of what Hūd says; the prepositions ʿan and bāʾ can substitute for one another.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p11/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Bayyina means a proof, and is so called because it makes truth distinct from falsehood.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p11/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Though Hūd had shown miracles, his ignorant opponents denied them and claimed he had shown none.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p11/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Al-Rāzī calls their reasoning poor: since they admitted God alone benefits and harms and idols do neither, reason itself should lead them to abandon idol worship, not merely Hūd's word.
[RAZI-FULL:v18p11/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Their flat refusal to believe Hūd indicates persistence in blind imitation and denial.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:50-54/r21] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | They say Hūd brought no clear proof or argument.
[QURTUBI-FULL:11:50-54/r22] QURTUBI-FULL, d. 671 · author | holds | Their refusal to believe him is stubborn persistence in unbelief.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:53-55/r1] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They deny proof out of extreme obstinacy and disregard even the miracles brought to them.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:53-55/r2] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | They refuse to abandon their idols’ worship at Hud’s word; the phrase describes their state as they refuse.
[BAYDAWI-FULL:11:53-55/r3] BAYDAWI-FULL, d. 685 · author | holds | Their words are meant to make Hud despair of their response or belief.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p160/r1] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | Their claim that Hūd brought no proof is a lie despite the many signs; Quraysh made a similar demand of the Prophet.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p160/r2] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | The clause is circumstantial to the pronoun in “abandoning”: they will not leave their gods on the basis of his word.
[NASAFI-FULL:v2p160/r3] NASAFI-FULL, d. 710 · author | holds | They say people of their standing cannot believe someone like Hūd, trying to make him despair of their response.
[QASHANI:11:52-53/r5] QASHANI, d. 736 · author | holds | They deny Hud's clear proof because natural veils limit their understanding and blind their inner sight, preventing them from grasping its demonstration.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r1] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | بينة means a clear proof or argument demonstrating the truth of Hud's claim.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | Hud's opponents lie when they claim he brought no proof, just as Quraysh did, since Hud and other prophets had miracles even if not all are specified here.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | reports | Another explanation is that their blindness to tru

th and failure to consider the signs made them deny that any sign was a sign.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r4] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · النبي | reports | The Prophet says every prophet received signs of a kind through which people believed; no grading is stated here.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r5] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · الزمخشري | reports | Zamakhshari parses عن قولك as a circumstantial phrase attached to the pronoun in تاركي: they would leave their gods departing from your saying.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r6] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn Atiyya takes عن as causal, attached to تاركي: Hud's unsupported word would not cause them to abandon their gods. | mentions 9:114
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r7] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The next clause reinforces the opponents' effort to extinguish Hud's hope that they will enter his religion.
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v6p167/r8] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | They explain Hud's call to worship Allah alone as madness inflicted by their gods because he insulted them and urged people to abandon their worship.
[SAMIN-DURR:11:53/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | ببينة may attach to جئتنا, meaning they were shown no proof, or modify an omitted state such as مستقرا or ملتبسا ببينة.
[SAMIN-DURR:11:53/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | prefers | عن قولك is preferably circumstantial from the pronoun in تاركي, meaning they leave their idols while turning from his statement; alternatively عن is causal and attaches to تاركي. | mentions 9:114
[SAMIN-DURR:11:53/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · ابن عطية | reports | Ibn ʿAṭiyya suggests a causal عن, while al-Zamakhsharī mentions only the preferred circumstantial analysis. | mentions 9:114
[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v4p329#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · author | holds | Hud's people say he brought no proof, they will not abandon their gods merely because he tells them to, and they will not believe him.
[BURHAN:v3p336/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | Hud shifts from the statement “I call God to witness” to the command “you witness”: God's testimony affirms monotheism, while addressing the idolaters this way shows disregard for their religion.
[BURHAN:v4p286/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | ʿAn can mark cause: Abraham's prayer followed a promise, and Lot's people say they will not abandon their gods because of Muhammad's statement.
[NASHR:v1p294/r2] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | When the letter before mīm has a vowel, mīm before bā is made quiescent and concealed with nasalization to avoid successive vowels; when the preceding letter is quiescent, the general rule is to leave it clear.
[NASHR:v1p294/r3] NASHR, d. 833 · القصباني عن شجاع عن أبي عمرو | reports | Al-Qasbani from Shuja from Abu Amr reports concealment after a madd or lin letter, but this route is outside the book’s transmissions.
[NASHR:v1p294/r4] NASHR, d. 833 · author | rejects | Some earlier scholars called this concealment idgham; the author says ikhfa is the correct term and defers fuller discussion.
[NASHR:v1p294/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into rāʾ or lām when the preceding letter is vowelled, but remains clear when the preceding letter is quiescent.
[NASHR:v1p294/r6] NASHR, d. 833 · أصحاب اليزيدي عن أبي عمرو | reports | They assimilate the final nūn of نحن into lām only in ten occurrences; other than this word, a quiescent preceding letter prevents assimilation.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r1] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | After Hūd gave advice with utmost clarity and showed signs that would ordinarily convince people, the only answer was rejection.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r2] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Calling him by his bare name instead of an honorific expresses harshness and rudeness.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r3] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Their denial shows obstinate resistance to clear reason and transmitted proof, like the Arabs' demand for a sign despite the Prophet's innumerable signs (13:7). | mentions 13:7
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r4] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | They say they will neither move beyond nor turn away from their idols because of Hūd's statement.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r5] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Biqāʿī notes their use of waw instead of causal fa, which would make the first statement the cause of the second.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r6] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | The emphatic negation and nominal sentence portray settled defiance; they refuse to follow Hūd out of obstinacy rather than sincere belief that he lacked a proof.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r7] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | Bayyina is a clear proof that distinguishes truth from falsehood; bayān separates a meaning from others until it is clarified to the mind.
[BIQAI-FULL:v3p542/r8] BIQAI-FULL, d. 885 · author | holds | People reject manifest proofs by suppressing doubt, imitating leaders, accusing the source, adopting corrupt premises, or acting from envy; all these causes share the presence of doubt.
[ITQAN:v1p252/r5] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Nūn assimilates into rā or lām after a vowel and is otherwise clear, except nūn in naḥnu, which assimilates because it recurs often, repeats nūn, stays vocalized, and is heavy.
[ITQAN:v2p479/r3] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | عن can express cause: the people will not leave their gods because of Hud's words, and Abraham's prayer was because of a promise.
[ITQAN:v3p152#3/r1] ITQAN, d. 911 · author | holds | Concision can arise from restriction, conjunction, passive voice, pronouns, a verb governing a complement clause, ellipsis in coordination or objects, interrogative and conditional particles, generic words, and dual or plural forms.
[ITQAN:v3p152#3/r2] ITQAN, d. 911 · ابن أبي الإصبع | reports | Ibn Abi al-Isba also counts interpretive breadth as a form of concision: wording supports several possible meanings, as with the openings of sūras.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r10] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | They will not believe Hud's call to monotheism and abandoning idols, expressly extinguishing his hope that they will respond.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r3] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | قالوا begins a new answer, with an implied question asking what Hud's people said after his commands and prohibitions.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r4] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | They deny receiving proof despite the miracles, out of extreme obstinacy, like Quraysh asking for a sign after many signs had come. | mentions 13:7
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r5] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | They mean they will not abandon worship of their idols.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r6] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The nūn of تاركين is dropped because the active participle is annexed to آلهتنا.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r7] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | عن قولك is a circumstantial phrase tied to the pronoun in تاركي: they will not leave their idols because of Hud's words.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r8] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · author | holds | The circumstantial wording makes Hud's words the effective cause of their leaving, a nuance stronger than ب or ل would convey.
[BURSEVI:v4p91#2/r9] BURSEVI, d. 1127 · السعدي المفتي | reports | Al-Saʿdi al-Mufti suggests that عن can mean بسبب, as in the verse about Abraham's promise. | mentions 9:114
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The people of Hud deny he brought clear proof either from stubborn resistance or because they are so blind to truth and inattentive to the signs that they misjudge a miracle; the prophets in fact brought manifest signs and miracles.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r10] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | They mean either that they do not believe what Hud brought or that they believe nothing he says or does, which includes his message.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | They repeat their refusal to believe with a nominal sentence, added bā, and a fronted subject for emphasis, signaling that no hope of their believing remains.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · النبي | reports | A prophetic report says every prophet was given signs of the kind by which people believed; al-Alusi invokes it to explain that the signs were real even when this passage does not name them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Leaving their gods means abandoning worship of them, and they say they will not do so because of Hud's bare assertion, unsupported by proof; here 'an' marks causation and attaches to 'leaving.' | mentions 9:114
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعض المحققين | reports | Some careful grammarians attach the prepositional phrase to an omitted circumstantial 'departing from,' rather than directly to 'leaving.'
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The terms for departing from and returning to water became metaphors for acting and conducting affairs; a cited line uses issuing and drawing water as a metaphor for sound judgment in managing matters.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Arabic can omit the word for returning to water because departure entails it, as in the saying that someone acts only on another's judgment; the phrase then means they will not leave their gods while acting on Hud's word.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | On that analysis, negation applies both to the restriction and the main clause: they will neither leave their gods nor act on Hud's saying.
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view takes 'departing' to mean turning away, as a restriction on the negation, so they deny leaving their gods while turning away from Hud's words; it also answers Hud's command not to turn away. | mentions 11:52
[ALUSI-FULL:v12p81#2/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · بعضهم | reports | Some analyze the construction as semantic inclusion rather than an omitted complement; al-Zamakhshari's wording appears to support this, as al-Kashf explains.

ALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Hud's people say he brought no clear proof, refuse to abandon their idols at his word, and refuse to believe him.

[TABATABAI:11:50-60#2/r7] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | God sent a barren, furious wind through adverse days, lasting seven nights and eight days; it left the people fallen like hollow palm trunks and destroyed them all but their dwellings.

[TABATABAI:11:50-60#2/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Hūd was from ʿĀd and the second prophet whose struggle against idolatry and suffering for God the Quran narrates; God praises him among the noble messengers.
